name: Step One: Social Class
notes:
Though not all nations and societies have the same kind of social ordering, many nations and cultures have social hierarchies consisting primarily of commoners and nobility. These social classes are determined by a character's parents and the social class that they've been born into, and dictate much of a character's life and perspective. Because social class is a construct that is imposed upon each character by the society they live in, there are no features or abilities inherent to a person of any particular class. However, social class can often limit a character's choices when it comes to what kind of life they want to pursue, as well as limiting the ways they can interact with others and the society they live in. These class limitations are represented by a single Trait, either "noble" or "commoner", and the effects of their social class can weigh heavily on a character with the skills and ambition for a path that their status would make difficult for them.

Each social class provides characters with a Value and two points to put into the two Attributes that are listed with that class. When choosing your character's social class, you should pick the one that they were born into. Of course, within this simplified breakdown of class there are many complications, exceptions, and deviations from the rule (e.g. a nobleman's son who's run away from home and settled as a farmer). If you wish to create a character that moves or has moved between these categories or perhaps exists outside them, choose the class that best reflects how others would perceive your character at first glance.

While your character's social class will automatically become a Trait, the legitimacy or, perhaps more importantly, the illegitimacy of one's birth also functions as a Trait. Illegitimate children are often a source of shame for their parents (though this can also depend on the social status of the parents, as some nobles are so powerful they may feel above such judgements), and they are sometimes ignored, treated poorly, or even abandoned because of it. If your character was born out of wedlock, they gain the Trait "Illegitimate," and though this may not be easily perceivable to others, it can impact your character's experience in society and serves as a prompt for the Gamemaster to affect a character differently when they interact with others.

options.name: Commoner (Peasant)
options.description: The lowest on the hierarchy of social class, peasants are commoners who labor for a living. They typically don't own any land, instead paying rent to landlords (usually minor nobility) in exchange for getting to live on the land and cultivate it. This social class also encompasses skilled laborers like bakers, blacksmiths, and leatherworkers.

grants.valuePrompt: Reflect how the character perceives their place in the social hierarchy, and the lessons they've learned as a result. Example: 'Commoners must protect each other when the highborn won't.'

options.name: Commoner (Merchant)
options.description: Though still commoners, the merchant class exists higher on the social ladder than peasants due mainly to one thing: wealth. Those of the merchant class (bankers, artists, scholars, lawyers, priests, etc) are wealthy enough to own property and wield influence over politics and trade.

grants.valuePrompt: Reflect how the character perceives their place in the social hierarchy, and the lessons they've learned as a result. Example: "I can prove I'm as good as any nobleman."

options.name: Petty Nobility
options.description: Above the common classes, but at the bottom of the nobility, the petty nobility is made up of minor nobles, often those who have been ennobled by a duke or monarch but without their own lands to control (e.g. knights, baronets, etc).

grants.valuePrompt: Reflect how the character perceives their place in the social hierarchy, and the lessons they've learned as a result. Example: 'I owe a debt to Lord Fife, and I will repay it.'

options.name: Landed Nobility
options.description: Landed nobility are powerful aristocrats who control their own territories and hold their own courts, though still owe their fealty to an overlord, typically a monarch. Titles and territories are typically passed down to descendants.

grants.valuePrompt: Reflect how the character perceives their place in the social hierarchy, and the lessons they've learned as a result. Example: 'The hierarchy of nobility is the natural order of things, and upholding it preserves peace.'

options.name: Royalty
options.description: Obviously at the top of the social hierarchy, members of the royalty are the sovereigns of territories or nations, whose families have been invested with power by the divine right of kings, or merely by virtue of dynasty.

grants.valuePrompt: Reflect how the character perceives their place in the social hierarchy, and the lessons they've learned as a result. Example: 'It is better to be feared than loved.'
